capabilities.target: Private repositories owned by the user
Public repository (readable by anyone on GitHub, including the issue author)

inputs.source: User's direct prompt in the desktop client
Open issue content in the public repository; any GitHub user can author it

elements.name: Public issue content entering the agent as tool output
Public GitHub users (any account can open issues)
Pull request creation on the public repository

controls.name: Per-tool-call client approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees a collapsed summary rather than the raw destination and payload (model_summary review mode), so a more persuasive model can describe a malicious action benignly (ASI09). Users approve many calls per session, which produces approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403) independent of any single model upgrade.

controls.name: Least-privilege, repo-scoped GitHub token
controls.decay_rationale: A token scoped only to the public repository would make the private-repo read capability unreachable from this workflow regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Pinned/hashed MCP server image and tool definitions
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning the container digest and hashing tool schemas prevents a rug-pull style redefinition of tools after the user has approved the server.

controls.name: Raw-action approval with cross-boundary flagging
controls.decay_rationale: Showing the approver the full destination, repo, and payload instead of a collapsed summary, and flagging any call chain that reads private data and writes to a public destination, removes dependence on the model's own description of the action.

controls.name: Non-model filtering of imperative instructions in issue text
controls.decay_rationale: A non-model filter stripping imperative language from untrusted issue text narrows the injection surface, but obfuscated or multi-turn instructions can still get through, so this is defense in depth rather than a severing control.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): malicious public issue drives private-repo read and public-PR exfiltration

attack_path.note: Untrusted instructions embedded in an issue anyone on GitHub can open.
Agent follows the injected instruction and reads confidential content from a private repository, using the broad-scope PAT.
Agent opens a pull request on the public repository containing the private content, readable by anyone, completing the exfiltration.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: The approval prompt is changed to auto-approve or 'always allow', the model backing the agent is upgraded without re-review, or per-session approval volume rises further.

evidence.observation: GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN is passed into the github-mcp-server container; runtime notes confirm it has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private.
'Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository,' making issue content an untrusted source that reaches the agent's context.
'The client asks for approval per tool call. Arguments are collapsed by default. Users approve many calls per session,' making the approval gate model_summary review mode at high volume.

recommendations.action: Issue a fine-grained, least-privilege GitHub token scoped to only the public repository for this workflow, so the private-repo read capability is unreachable from issue-triage tasks.

Change the approval prompt to show the full raw action (destination repo, diff, and payload) rather than a collapsed summary, and require explicit confirmation for any call chain that reads private data and then writes to a public destination.
Pin the MCP server container to a specific digest and hash tool schemas to prevent silent redefinition.
Add a non-model filter over untrusted issue text to flag or strip imperative instructions before they reach the model, as defense in depth.

findings.title: Unpinned, unverified MCP server enables supply-chain tool redefinition (ASI04)

forecast.watch_signal: The docker image digest changes without a corresponding review, or the approval prompt is disabled or changed to auto-approve.

evidence.observation: docker run args reference 'ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server' with no digest or version tag, so the image resolves to whatever 'latest' currently points to.
The server is launched locally with a static GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN env var; no separate peer identity verification step for the server image itself is described.

recommendations.action: Pin the container to a specific digest and verify tool schema hashes before trusting them.
Scope the token narrowly so that even a compromised server cannot reach private repositories.

stride_coverage.rationale: Artifacts do not describe how the agent process itself authenticates to the user's client, so spoofing of the agent process is not assessed.
autonomy.can_modify_own_config is false and no capability writes to the agent's own configuration in this design.
Artifacts do not describe any logging or audit trail of tool invocations by the agent, so attributability of its actions is unknown.
Artifacts do not describe rate limits, spend caps, or step limits for the agent's tool-calling loop, so resource exhaustion risk is not assessed.
Artifacts do not describe server-side logging of tool invocations, so repudiation risk for the MCP server process is not assessed.
Artifacts do not describe any rate limiting on the MCP server itself, so denial of service risk is not assessed.
This flow carries the principal's own trusted prompt and does not cross a trust boundary, so cross-boundary tampering analysis does not apply here.
This is an inbound flow carrying issue text into the agent; it does not carry data out of the trust boundary, so outbound disclosure through this specific flow does not apply.
Artifacts do not describe whether repeated or flooding issue creation could exhaust agent processing capacity, so this is not assessed.
GitHub's own user identity and audit systems govern issue authorship and are outside this agent design's control boundary.
Artifacts do not describe any rate limit on pull request creation, so repeated use for resource exhaustion is not assessed.
Artifacts do not describe whether the token value itself can be overwritten or rotated maliciously, so tampering of the credential store is not assessed.
Artifacts do not describe rate limits on GitHub API usage tied to this token, so denial of service through quota exhaustion is not assessed.
Only a read capability (cap.read_private_repo) is declared against this store in this design; no write path is defined, so tampering via this agent is not applicable.
Artifacts do not describe any limit on how much private repository content can be read in a session, so this is not assessed.

rating.rationale: The design matches the public GitHub MCP exfiltration pattern (TC1, lethal trifecta): a single broad-scope personal access token grants the agent read access to the user's private repositories and write access to the public repository, while the public repository's issues are open to any GitHub user (untrusted input). Inherent risk is critical (untrusted source to a severe sink). The only declared control is a per-tool-call approval prompt that shows a collapsed summary rather than raw arguments and is approved at high volume per session; the rubric credits this one tier with a floor of moderate, giving a residual of high. Under model upgrade, autonomy increase, or removal of the approval gate, that control fails and the forecast returns to critical. A secondary property finding covers the unpinned, unverified MCP server image, which is an independent supply-chain path to the same two capabilities.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the MCP config and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt or tool-level instructions were provided beyond the user's initial request, so prompt-based behavioral controls could not be assessed.
The actual scope of the GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN was not independently verified against GitHub's token settings; it is taken as declared in the runtime notes (confidence: medium).
The github-mcp-server's full tool set and descriptions were not provided; the capability inventory is inferred from the two tool references given in the case (get_file_contents, create_pull_request).
